DCM is heterogeneous in both genetic architecture and clinical expression. Rare, high-impact variants explain a meaningful subset of cases, while common variants and environmental stressors modulate penetrance and age at onset (Table 2). The strongest single-gene contributors in adult disease are titin truncating variants, followed by lamin A/C and a set of arrhythmia-prone genes that carry management implications. Contemporary guidelines recognise a group of genotypes that confer higher arrhythmic risk, which should influence device decisions alongside conventional clinical markers. These include LMNA, FLNC truncating variants, RBM20 hotspot variants, PLN variants, and selected desmosomal genes such as DSP and TMEM43, even when left ventricular ejection fraction is only mildly reduced or borderline normal.
Titin truncating variants

Heterozygous TTN truncating variants, particularly those situated in exons that are constitutively expressed in adult myocardium, account for around 15 to 25 percent of non-ischaemic DCM, compared with much lower frequencies in controls. Pathophysiology involves a combination of haploinsufficiency and truncated protein effects, with disease expression shaped by the position of the variant, exon usage, and additional stressors. Clinical translation centres on careful variant curation use gene-specific considerations.
Lamin A/C and conduction disease

Late gadolinium enhancement sequence in a patient with Lamin A/C cardiomyopathy (LMNA (+), Exon 1 p.Arg541His), showing a markedly dilated left ventricle with near transmural LGE in the anterolateral and inferolateral segments and mid-myocardial LGE in the anteroseptal and inferoseptal segments.
Fig. 1a
Left bundle branch block.
Fig. 1b

LMNA pathogenic variants account for a much smaller proportion of DCM than TTN but carry a disproportionate burden of arrhythmic and conduction events (Fig. 1a, Fig. 1bA and B). Risk of sustained ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death begins at higher ejection fractions than in other forms of DCM. Predictive tools, including the LMNA-VTA score, can guide earlier device therapy, particularly when non-sustained VT, male sex, non-missense variants, or atrioventricular block are present. Conduction disease, atrial arrhythmias, and rapid progression are common.
RBM20 cardiomyopathy

RBM20 encodes a splicing factor with a well-defined hotspot in the RS domain, especially the RSRSP motif in and around amino acids 634 to 638. Hotspot missense variants are associated with early-onset DCM, high arrhythmic burden, and male predominance in some cohorts. Mechanistic data indicate that RS-domain variants disrupt nuclear localisation and promote cytoplasmic condensates, which may amplify disease beyond splicing defects alone. Clinically, RBM20 should be considered an arrhythmic DCM genotype, and primary prevention ICD may be reasonable at higher LVEF than conventional thresholds when additional risk factors are present.
FLNC truncating variants

Truncating variants in FLNC produce a left-sided arrhythmogenic phenotype that overlaps DCM and non-dilated LV scar cardiomyopathy. Patients often show extensive subepicardial or mid-wall LGE on CMR, ventricular arrhythmias out of proportion to chamber size, and a risk profile that justifies proactive ICD strategies. Cohort and pooled analyses consistently link FLNC truncations to malignant ventricular arrhythmias and heart failure progression.
PLN variants

The phospholamban p.Arg14del founder variant is a major cause of DCM and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in the Netherlands and occurs a separate, independently arising introduction has been documented in a Greek family as well.. Phenotypes include ventricular arrhythmias, low-voltage ECGs, and fibrofatty scar that mimics arrhythmogenic disease. Arrhythmia risk can be substantial despite modest reductions in LVEF, which again supports earlier ICD consideration in selected carriers.
Desmosomal and cytoskeletal genes with DCM overlap

Desmoplakin cardiomyopathy is increasingly recognised as a left-dominant arrhythmogenic disorder with recurrent myocarditis-like "hot phases," chest pain, troponin rise, and characteristic ring-like LV fibrosis on CMR. These inflammatory episodes correlate with subsequent ventricular arrhythmias and heart failure events, so recognition should prompt exercise modification, rhythm surveillance, and consideration of device therapy when appropriate. Cytoskeletal genes such as DES and BAG3 contribute to DCM and mixed phenotypes with conduction disease and skeletal myopathy.
SCN5A and electrical-mechanical overlap

SCN5A, classically linked to conduction disease and Brugada syndrome, can present as an arrhythmogenic DCM with substantial atrial and ventricular arrhythmia. Conduction disease that precedes LV dilation, family history of sudden death, and mixed electrical phenotypes should raise suspicion. In such families, genotype-informed counselling and earlier device planning may be warranted. A MEPPC (Multifocal Ectopic Purkinje-related Premature Contractions) phenotype is driven by autosomal-dominant, gain-of-function SCN5A variants that hyper-excite Purkinje fibers leading to multifocal PVCs, which typically respond to sodium-channel blockers.
Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) genetics
Late gadolinium enhancement sequence in a patient with arrythmogenic cardiomyopathy (JUP p.Gln317Pro) showing ring like LGE pattern.
Fig. 2a
Atrial fibrillation and low voltage QRS complexes. Poor R wave progression V1-V4.
Fig. 2b

PKP2 is the most frequent gene in classic right dominant ACM. DSP, DSG2, DSC2, and JUP contribute across the spectrum. Non desmosomal contributors include TMEM43, PLN, DES, and FLNC. Left dominant and biventricular forms are increasingly recognised, and myocarditis like presentations are common early in disease (Fig. 2a, Fig. 2bA-B).

The Padua criteria integrate morphology, tissue characterisation, ECG or arrhythmia features, and family or genetic findings. Cardiac MRI adds value through scar patterns that differ from sarcomeric disease.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) genetics

RCM may be caused by sarcomeric genes such as TNNI3, TNNT2, MYH7, and MYBPC3, and by cytoskeletal genes including DES, FLNC, and BAG3. Overlap with HCM or DCM is common, and many families display mixed phenotypes across generations. Recognition depends on biatrial enlargement, normal or small ventricles, and marked diastolic dysfunction. Arrhythmic risk varies with genotype and scar burden.

Danon disease is an X linked autophagic myopathy due to LAMP2 variants. Males typically present in adolescence with severe hypertrophy and high arrhythmic risk, while females present later with variable expression (Fig. 4a, Fig. 4bA-B). Multisystem features include skeletal myopathy and cognitive involvement. Emerging gene transfer approaches are under study, but clinical management currently focuses on early detection, rhythm surveillance, and heart failure therapies.
Fabry disease (GLA)

Fabry disease is an X linked lysosomal disorder with cardiac hypertrophy, conduction disease, and arrhythmias alongside renal and neurological involvement, caused by pathogenic variants in GLA, leading to deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A. Late onset cardiac variants are common. Diagnosis rests on enzyme activity and genetic testing, with lyso Gb3 supporting disease activity. Enzyme replacement and chaperone therapy for amenable variants can stabilise or improve cardiac parameters if started early.
Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy

Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy results from impaired oxidative phosphorylation due to pathogenic variants in mitochondrial DNA or nuclear genes that encode mitochondrial proteins. Common mtDNA causes include the m.3243A > G variant in MT-TL1 which is frequent in MELAS-spectrum disease and is well linked to hypertrophic or mixed cardiomyopathy with conduction and arrhythmic involvement.
Pompe disease (GAA)

Pompe disease spans infantile onset cardiomyopathy with severe hypertrophy and late onset forms with milder cardiac involvement. It is caused by pathogenic variants in GAA, leading to deficiency of acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase). Enzyme replacement therapy improves survival and cardiomyopathy metrics.
clinical translation

The 2022 EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS Expert Consensus, endorsed across Europe, North America, Asia-Pacific, and Latin America, summarises indications and workflows for cardiovascular genetic testing, including patient selection, informed consent, test choice (targeted vs panel), laboratory standards, variant classification, and family management.
When to test and what to order

Indications include a clinical diagnosis of cardiomyopathy, unexplained ventricular arrhythmias, conduction disease in young individuals, and family history of early cardiac events. Targeted, evidence-based panels aligned to ClinGen validity curation are preferable to very broad lists. Include copy number analysis for genes with known deletions or duplications.
Pretest counselling and return of results

Counselling should cover potential outcomes, including pathogenic, likely pathogenic, variant of uncertain significance, or negative. Consent should address incidental findings and data sharing. Return of results should include written interpretation, a family letter, and a plan for re-review.
Variant interpretation and reclassification

Use ACMG or AMP criteria with ClinGen SVI updates for strength adjustments and functional evidence. Weigh population frequency against penetrance, consider segregation, and apply disease or gene specific classifications where available. Maintain a reanalysis cadence as databases grow. It is also important to build and curate a national variant database, as pathogenic and founder variants can be country or ancestry-specific and are often under-represented in global resources.
Cascade screening of relatives

Offer cascade testing to first degree relatives when a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant is found. For HCM, adolescents typically undergo annual or biennial screening, while adults are re-screened every few years or sooner if symptomatic, with adjustments for athletic participation and pregnancy. Provide age-appropriate ECG, echocardiography, and, when indicated, CMR and rhythm monitoring.
Risk stratification and devices

Genotype informs ICD thresholds in select DCM genes. LMNA, FLNC truncation, RBM20, and PLN variants (in particular the Arg14del variant) carry sufficiently high arrhythmic risk to support proactive ICD planning in the presence of additional risk features, even at ejection fraction values above traditional cut points. HCM decisions rely on clinical risk models and imaging, with genotype an adjunct rather than a sole trigger. ACM device strategy weighs syncope, arrhythmia history, scar burden, and genotype.
Therapeutic implications
For phenocopies, disease specific therapies include enzyme replacement or chaperones in Fabry and Pompe, while clinical trials in Danon and other rare disorders continue.
Conclusion

Genetic practice has moved from adjunct to anchor in the care of inherited cardiomyopathies, clarifying aetiology, refining risk, and opening targeted therapies while guiding families through cascade screening and life planning. Sarcomeric disease in HCM, arrhythmogenic genotypes in DCM and ACM, and overlapping restrictive phenotypes can now be approached with curated panels, copy number detection, and escalation to genome and RNA when needed. Phenocopies such as PRKAG2, Danon, Fabry, mitochondrial disease, and Pompe require active case finding because timely, disease specific treatment and device strategy can change outcomes. Variant classification must follow standardised frameworks with planned re review, and genotype should inform but not overrule clinical judgement in device and treatment decisions. Polygenic scores are promising as modifiers yet remain adjuncts. Priorities for the next few years include broader ancestry representation, reliable data sharing, equitable access to testing and therapies, and rigorous evaluation of emerging gene targeted approaches. With these foundations, cardiovascular genetics can deliver practical, humane care for patients and families.

passages.text: A 3.3-A cryo-EM structure of an engineered high-affinity human prothrombinase complex*
Key Points
Cryo-EM structure reveals a large interface involving the EGF2 and serine protease domains of fXa and the A2 and A3 domains of fVa.
The a2-loop at the C-terminus of the A2 domain makes critical contacts with the heparin-binding site of fXa.
Visual Abstract
Abstract

Thrombin is generated from prothrombin through cleavage at 2 sites by the enzyme prothrombinase, composed of factor Xa (fXa) and fVa. The affinity of fXa for fVa is low, with assembly and function dependent on phospholipid (PL) membranes. Some snakes have evolved venom versions of fXa that bind to fVa with high affinity and efficiently activate prothrombin in the absence of PL. We created a similar high-affinity, PL-independent human prothrombinase with 17 mutations to human fXa (M17). The increase in affinity enabled cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure determination of M17-prothrombinase to a resolution of 3.3 A. All protein domains were well resolved in the map, except for the gamma-carboxyglutamic acid domain of fXa. The main contacts involve the serine protease and epidermal growth factor-like domain 2 (EGF2) domains of fXa and the A2 and A3 domains of fVa, resulting in the burying of a total surface area of 4900 A2. The map is of sufficient quality to resolve side-chain interactions, including several key M17 mutations. To aid in the placement of the loop C-terminal to the A2 domain (a2-loop), we solved a high-resolution crystal structure of fXa in complex with a synthetic a2 peptide. The acidic a2-loop interacts with the basic heparin-binding site of fXa, involving a conserved antiparallel beta-strand interaction. The M17-prothrombinase structure is compatible with data from biochemical and mutagenesis research and provides important new insights into the assembly and function of the prothrombinase complex.

Understanding how protein-protein interactions occur is central to modern drug development. Ustok and colleagues overcame a barrier to solving critical structural aspects of prothrombinase by engineering a human prothrombinase complex that assembles without membranes, allowing its high-resolution structural determination by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Their solution aligns with biochemical research and sheds new light on a critical protein-protein interaction with significant modulatory implications for hemostasis and anticoagulant development.
Introduction

Blood coagulation (hemostasis) is a highly regulated process that evolved hundreds of millions of years ago. Orthologs of the human hemostatic proteins are found in all vertebrates and are highly conserved across species. These proteins participate in the blood coagulation cascade that was first described in 1964 and are composed of serine proteases, their cofactors, and their substrates. The cascade of zymogen activation events can be triggered by different stimuli and serves to amplify thrombin production to ensure stable clot formation when vascular integrity is compromised. The dysregulation of thrombin production leads to bleeding disorders such as hemophilia and thrombotic disorders such as ischemic stroke and pulmonary embolism.

Schematics of fXa and fV domain organization and prothrombin processing pathways. (A) fXa is composed of a light (lavender) and a heavy chain (light blue) connected via a disulfide bond (dashed lines). The N-terminal Gla is followed by 2 EGF domains and a C-terminal SP domain. Although not depicted, rigid units are formed of the Gla/EGF1 and EGF2/SP domains through noncovalent interactions, with some flexibility at the linker between these units. (B) fV is a single-chain protein composed of 2 A domains (A1 and A2), a large unstructured B-domain, an A3 domain, and 2 membrane-binding C-domains (C1 and C2). The domains are colored from blue to red from the N- to C-terminus. The B-domain is excised by either thrombin or fXa cleavage at the 3 indicated sites, resulting in fVa, composed of a heavy (A1-A2) and a light (A3-C1-C2) chain. The loop linking the A1 and A2 domains is denoted a1, and the unstructured region following the A2 domain is known as the a2-loop. (C) Prothrombin (top) is composed of an N-terminal Gla domain, 2 kringle (K1 and K2) domains, and an SP domain (H). The K2 and H domains are linked by L, which is disulfide bonded to H. Cleavage at 2 positions (R271 and R320) is required for conversion to thrombin (bottom). The left pathway (intermediates F1.2 and Pre-2) is kinetically favored for fXa when not in complex with fVa, and the right pathway (meizothrombin intermediate) is favored when prothrombinase is assembled.

Enzymes have been identified in certain toxins that have the ability to generate thrombin activity, including from the venom of some snakes. However, in normal physiology, only the prothrombinase complex produces thrombin. Prothrombinase is composed of a serine protease, factor Xa (fXa), and a cofactor, fVa, that assemble on a phospholipid (PL) surface in the presence of calcium ions. fXa consists of an N-terminal gamma-carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) domain, 2 epidermal growth factor-like (EGF) domains and a chymotrypsin family serine protease domain (SP) (Figure 1A), and on its own is a poor activator of prothrombin. The essential cofactor fVa is generated from the procofactor fV through the proteolytic excision of its B-domain by thrombin or fXa and is composed of 3 A domains and 2 membrane-binding C domains (Figure 1B). The activation of both components is required for fXa and fVa to interact, but binding affinity is low in the absence of negatively charged PL membranes, with a dissociation constant in the micromolar range. PL membranes improve the affinity by ~1000-fold, and the assembly of prothrombinase accelerates thrombin generation by 300 000-fold over fXa alone. The PL surface thus plays an important regulatory role, helping to ensure that thrombin is only generated at sites of tissue damage where negatively charged phosphatidyl serine-rich surfaces are expressed.

Prothrombin is comprised of an N-terminal Gla domain, 2 kringle domains (K1 and K2), and an SP domain (H), organized into N-terminal (Gla/K1) and C-terminal (K2/H) structured regions connected by an unstructured linker of 26 residues in length (Figure 1C). The conversion of prothrombin to thrombin requires cleavage after Arg271 and Arg320 (Figure 1C). Cleavage at Arg271 severs the link between the membrane-anchoring F1.2 fragment (Gla/K1/K2) and the zymogen form of the SP domain, prethrombin-2 (Pre-2). Cleavage at Arg320 is the activating event that triggers the zymogen-to-protease conformational change (Arg320-Ile321 is 15-16 in chymotrypsin numbering) and preserves the linkage with F1.2 due to the presence of a disulfide bond. fXa on its own cleaves prothrombin initially at Arg271, forming F1.2 and Pre-2 as intermediates, with a much slower cleavage of Arg320. When prothrombinase is assembled, the order of cleavage is reversed and the main intermediate is the membrane-anchored active protease meizothrombin; the second cleavage at Arg271 is processive, with only the transient appearance of meizothrombin evident by sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE).

Despite decades of research, fundamental questions regarding the cofactor function of fVa remain, including: what is the role of the PL membrane surface in prothrombinase assembly and function; how does fXa interact with fVa; how does fVa accelerate cleavage of prothrombin and impose initial cleavage at Arg320; and how is processivity conferred? We previously reported on the creation of a high-affinity variant of fXa with 17 mutations (M17), which was based on a model of prothrombinase built on a crystal structure of the snake venom prothrombinase, pseutarin C, and guided by sequence differences with a high-affinity fXa ortholog hopsarin D. This variant binds to fVa with a dissociation constant of ~20nM and converts prothrombin to thrombin via meizothrombin in the absence of PL membranes. To assess the role of PL membranes in prothrombinase assembly and function, we further characterized the M17 variant to determine its rate constants of fVa binding and the influence of PL membranes on prothrombin processing. The M17-fVa complex was then used to generate a 3.3-A cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) map, which satisfyingly resolves the question of how fXa and fVa interact to form prothrombinase and provides a new framework for addressing the other questions relating to the cofactor functions of fVa.
Methods
Recombinant protein expression and purification

Wild-type (WT) human fX, full-length M17 fX, and B-domainless fV were expressed, purified, and activated as described previously. For grid preparation, M17 fXa was inhibited by Glu-Gly-Arg-chloromethyl ketone (EGRCK; Prolytix) and dialyzed into a buffer containing 20mM HEPES (N-2-hydroxyethylpiperazine-N'-2-ethanesulfonic acid) at pH 7.5, 150mM NaCl, and 5mM CaCl2. Truncated human fX (EGF2-SP) was expressed in Escherichia coli as inclusion bodies and refolded, purified, and activated as previously described. Protein used in crystallization trials was inhibited with EGRCK and desalted into a buffer containing 10mM Tris at pH 7.4, 200mM NaCl, and 5muM CaCl2. Recombinant human prothrombin (S195A) was prepared as described previously.
Assessment of binding rates of M17 to fVa

An Octet Red biolayer interferometry instrument was used to determine binding rates. All experiments were performed in a binding buffer (20mM HEPES at pH 7.4, 150mM NaCl, 2mM CaCl2, 0.1% bovine serum albumin, and 0.1% PEG8000) using streptavidin-coated biosensors. M17 was treated with biotinylated EGRCK, desalted, and loaded onto the biosensors at 2.0 mug/mL. Remaining biotin-binding sites were quenched with biocytin (50 mug/mL). fVa was diluted in the binding buffer to concentrations between 4nM and 64nM. A no-analyte reference biosensor was used as a control for baseline drift. Data traces were fit using Prism (version 10.5.0; GraphPad).
Prothrombin processing monitored by SDS-PAGE

Reactions were initiated by adding fXa or M17 (2nM) to a solution containing 5muM S195A prothrombin and 30nM fVa (final concentrations) in an assay buffer (20mM Tris at pH 7.4, 150mM NaCl, 2mM CaCl2, and 0.1% PEG8000) with or without 20muM phosphatidylcholine:phosphatidylethanolamine:phosphatidylserine (60:20:20) vesicles. Samples (10muL) were withdrawn at indicated time points and quenched by mixing with 10 muL of SDS sample buffer containing 100mM dithiothreitol and 100muM 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonyl fluoride hydrochloride (AEBSF), followed by incubation at 95 C for 5 minutes. Samples were run on 4% to 12% BisTris gradient gels (Invitrogen) with MOPS (4-morpholinepropanesulfonic acid) buffer (Formedium). Bands were visualized by staining with Quick Coomassie Stain (Generon) at room temperature for 1 hour, destained, and imaged on a ChemiDoc MP Imaging System (Bio-Rad). Densitometry analysis was performed using Image Lab software (Bio-Rad). Two independent experiments were conducted, and kinetic analysis was performed using Prism.
Cryo-EM grid preparation, data collection, processing, and refinement

M17-prothrombinase was formed by mixing fVa with EGRCK-inhibited M17 at a 1:6 molar ratio to final concentrations of 862nM fVa and 5.17muM M17 in 20mM HEPES at pH 7.5, 150mM NaCl, and 5mM CaCl2. UltrAuFoil (R0.6/1 300 mesh) grids were glow discharged in residual air at 25 mA for 60 seconds using a Pelco easiGlow. Samples (3 muL) were applied to the grids with a 10-second wait time, followed by blotting for 1 second using -7 blot force in a 100% humidity chamber at 4 C, followed by flash plunging into liquid ethane (-180 C) using a Vitrobot Mark IV. Grids were imaged using a Titan Krios electron microscope with a K3 camera (Gatan) at the University of Cambridge Department of Biochemistry Cryo-EM facility. Data were collected at 105 000x magnification (pixel size, 0.83 A), using a dose of 45.74 electrons/A2 and defocus values between -1.0 and -2.0mum.

An initial data set revealed a large particle orientation bias (supplemental Figure 1A, available on the Blood website) that adversely affected the quality of the map. A subsequent data set was collected with a tilted stage (-25 ) and was processed using cryoSPARC with improved orientation distribution (supplemental Figure 1B). Patch motion correction and patch contrast transfer function were first run using default parameters; exposures with an estimated contrast transfer function resolution fit higher than 5 A were discarded. Blob picker was used to pick and extract 5 255 277 particles in 300 x 300-pixel boxes. Several rounds of ab initio and heterogeneous refinements were used to filter out bad particles. A single round of masked 3-dimensional classification was run to discard fVa particles not complexed with fXa. A final set of 70 154 particles was reextracted in a 440 x 440 pixel box for running nonuniform refinement (default parameters) to generate the final map at a resolution of 3.28 A (supplemental Figure 2). Data collection, processing, and refinement statistics are provided in supplemental Table 1.
Preliminary model building of prothrombinase using rigid domains

To create a model of 2-chain fVa, we removed the B-domain from the deposited AlphaFold model of fV (AF-P12259-F1-v4) and renumbered it to reflect the mature protein. The model of fVa was then fit into the map using ChimeraX. The coordinates for the SP and EGF2 domains of fXa were obtained from a protein data bank deposition 3Q3K and fit into the map with ChimeraX. Coordinates for the Gla and EGF1 domains were obtained from the AlphaFold deposition for fX (AF-P00742-F1-v4), again edited to reflect mature protein numbering, and initially placed by superimposing the AlphaFold fX model onto the SP and EGF2 domains fit into the map. The Gla-EGF1 unit was then fit into the map using ChimeraX and linked to the EGF2 domain in Coot. The C1 and C2 domains were individually refined into the map using Rigidbody Zone in Coot to account for flexibility of these domains relative to the A domains. The M17 mutations were then made in fXa to create the starting model of M17-prothrombinase. When supported by the map, structural metal ions were added at previously identified positions in fXa and fVa. Iterative cycles of real-space refinement in Phenix and model building in Coot were conducted to arrive at a final model.
Crystallization of the fXa-a2-peptide complex

A peptide corresponding to the acidic portion of the a2-loop (CIPDDDEDSY*EIFEP; * indicates phosphorylation; Biomatik) was resuspended in 10mM Tris at pH 8.0 to a concentration of 2.5mM and treated with 5mM iodoacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich) to block the N-terminal sulfhydryl group. The complex was prepared by mixing protein and peptide at a 1:4 molar ratio, with EGRCK-inhibited fXa (EGF2-SP) at 10 mg/mL. Crystallization trials were performed using the vapor diffusion sitting drop method in 96-well MRC 2 drop crystallization plates (Swissci) into which commercial crystallization screens were predispensed. Drops were set up using the Mosquito LCP (TTP Labtech) by mixing 100nL of protein and 100nL of reservoir solutions. Plates were monitored using a Rock Imager 182 (Formulatrix). Initial crystals were obtained after 4 days in 0.1M imidazole at pH 7.0 and 50% MPD (2-methyl-2,4-pentanediol). Optimization was conducted in 24-well hanging-drop crystallization plates (Hampton Research), and diffraction quality crystals were obtained after a few days of incubation at 19 C from drops containing 1 muL protein and 1 muL precipitant (0.1M imidazole at pH 7.0 and 60% volume-to-volume ratio of MPD).
Diffraction data collection and processing

The fXa-a2-peptide crystals were scooped and flash-frozen directly in liquid nitrogen. X-ray diffraction data were collected at Diamond Light Source (Oxford, United Kingdom) using the beamline I04 (100K, wavelength 0.70979 A). Data processing was conducted using AIMLESS from the CCP4 suite. Molecular replacement was conducted in Phaser using 3IIT. Model building and refinement were conducted using Coot and Refmac, and structure validation was conducted using MolProbity. Processing and refinement statistics are presented in supplemental Table 2.
Results
Formation and function of M17-prothrombinase

The effect of the M17 mutations on prothrombinase assembly and function. (A) Biolayer interferometry traces of the on (0-600 seconds) and off (601-1800 seconds) phases of fVa (well) binding to biotinylated EGRCK-inhibited M17 (biosensor). The concentrations of fVa ranged from 4nM to 64nM with doubling at each step (from blue to red), with fits in black. (B) The fraction prothrombin remaining relative to t = 0 based on densitometry of SDS gels (as in panels C-F) is plotted for WT fXa (circles) and M17 (squares) with fVa in the absence (open symbols) and presence (closed symbols) of PL. Data are from 2 separate experiments with averages plotted and standard errors as bars. (C-F) SDS gels of prothrombin processing for WT fXa and M17 with fVa in the absence and presence of PL, as indicated. Molecular weight markers are in the first lane of each gel, followed by t = 0 (no added fXa) and other time points from 0.5 to 90 minutes as indicated. The samples were reduced, so the F1.2-L band corresponds to the initial cleavage of Arg320 (meizothrombin formation), and the other bands are as depicted in Figure 1C. MWt, molecular weight.

The affinity of M17 for fVa was characterized by biolayer interferometry to determine binding rate constants. Fits from 4 separate experiments (Figure 2A) yielded values of kon = 7.6 +- 1.1 x 104 M-1s-1 and koff = 1.7 +- 0.7 x 10-3 s-1, resulting in a calculated dissociation constant of 22 +- 6nM. Improvement in binding affinity for M17 relative to fXa is derived primarily from improvement in the on-rate (76-fold relative to a 2.5-fold decrease in off-rate). Colocalization of the WT components on the PL surface would be expected to have a similar effect on affinity through an increase in the rate of association.

To determine whether the mutations of M17 also recapitulate the effect of a PL surface on prothrombinase function, we followed prothrombin processing using SDS-PAGE for WT fXa and M17 with fVa in the absence and presence of PL vesicles (Figure 2C-F). Quantification of bands by densitometry allows for the calculation of the rate of prothrombin processing, best reflected by the loss of the prothrombin band with time (Figure 2B). Consistent with previous reports, WT fXa with fVa in the absence of PL cleaves prothrombin slowly (0.003 +- 0.002 per minute), with a calculated time to half reaction (t1/2) of ~200 minutes. The addition of PL increases the rate 57-fold (0.17 +- 0.01 per minute), yielding a t1/2 of 4 minutes. M17 with fVa processes prothrombin 33-times faster than WT fXa with fVa, at a rate approaching that of prothrombinase with PL (0.10 +- 0.01 per minute; t1/2 of 7 minutes). Interestingly, the addition of PL to M17 and fVa has no effect on the rate of prothrombin processing (0.09 +- 0.01 per minute). All conditions produce bands reflecting both the Pre-2 and meizothrombin intermediates, with PL reducing the Pre-2 pathway for both WT fXa and M17. These data suggest that the role of the PL surface is primarily to aid in the association of fXa with fVa. We conclude that the M17-fVa complex formed in the absence of PL possesses the structural features of membrane-associated WT prothrombinase required for prothrombin processing, and it is therefore appropriate for use in structural studies.
Cryo-EM structure of M17-prothrombinase

Stereo views of the cryo-EM maps of M17-prothrombinase. (A) The unsharpened map obtained from a tilted stage shows features expected of the calculated resolution of 3.3 A and excellent coverage of the prothrombinase model (domains are labeled and colored essentially as in Figure 1A-B, and the Ca2+ ions of the Gla domain are denoted by green balls). (B) A local resolution map calculated from half-maps is oriented as in panel A, with colors indicating resolution (blue = 2.7, cyan = 3.2, lime = 3.6, yellow = 4.0, and red = 4.6 A). Images were created using PyMol and ChimeraX.

As described in "Methods," we obtained an interpretable cryo-EM map of M17-prothrombinase at a nominal resolution of 3.28 A. The model of human prothrombinase generated from the structure of pseutarin C fit well into the map, supporting a conserved binding interface between fXa and fVa across distantly related species, and showed excellent coverage for all domains except the Gla domain of fXa (Figure 3A). The local resolution map (Figure 3B) is in agreement with the resolution estimated by the Fourier shell correlation plot (supplemental Figure 2).

The bulk of the fXa-fVa interface is between structured domains; however, one of the most important potential contacts involves the unstructured region C-terminal to the A2 domain, known as the "a2-loop." The a2-loop begins at residue Ile657 and runs until the activation cleavage site at Arg709 (53 residues). An acidic stretch at the beginning of the a2-loop has been implicated in prothrombinase activity and is highly conserved across species. In the structure of pseutarin C, the a2-loop was found to interact with the heparin-binding site (HBS) of the fXa ortholog. Evidence of a similar interaction is observed in the cryo-EM map of M17-prothrombinase (supplemental Figure 3), but the resolution did not support its unequivocal, in-register placement.

Placement of the a2-loop onto fXa. (A) The crystal structure of the a2-peptide (yellow sticks) bound to fXa (heavy chain colored blue to red from the N- to C-terminus), with electron density contoured at 1sigma (blue mesh). Superpositions are shown of the fXa-a2-peptide crystal structure (yellow sticks) with the AlphaFold solution (B), the pseutarin C structure (4BXW) (C), and the final refined a2-loop in the M17-prothrombinase cryo-EM structure (D) as magenta sticks. (E) The surface of the M17-prothrombinase structure is shown after fitting the rigid domains into an unsharpened map (fXa and fVa colored as in Figure 1). A portion of the map unfilled by rigid domains (semitransparent gray) extends from the C-terminus of the A2 domain (green) onto the surface of the HBS of fXa (cyan). The a2-loop (magenta sticks) is shown in its final position, with the map extending from the core region to the C-terminus of the A2 domain. Images were created using Pymol.

To help place the a2-loop into the cryo-EM map, we crystallized a truncated form of fXa (EGF2-SP) with a peptide corresponding to the a2-loop and obtained a 1.2 A structure (supplemental Table 2). The core region (EDSY*EIFE) interacts with the HBS of fXa as an anti-parallel beta-strand (Figure 4A), with flexibility preventing modeling of the rest of the peptide. The crystal structure is in excellent agreement with the AlphaFold prediction (Figure 4B) and the previous structure of pseutarin C (Figure 4C). The core fit nicely into the cryo-EM map with limited adjustment (Figure 4D-E) and was then linked to the C-terminus of the A2 domain while remaining within the map.
The M17-fVa interaction

Sharpened map with final model, highlighting key M17 interactions. (A) A stereo view of the sharpened map (semitransparent gray) and final model is shown, with color and orientation as in Figure 3, and domains labeled. Close-ups of the map with interactions centered on mutated M17 residues, including Arg90 (mutated from Ser) (B), Asn129 (mutated from Glu) (C), and Lys132 (mutated from Thr) (D). Domains are colored as in panel A, and interactions are depicted as red dashed lines with distances in angstroms. Images were created using Pymol.

Stereo views of the surface electrostatics of fVa and M17. (A) The contribution of electrostatics to the formation of prothrombinase is illustrated by coloring the surface of fVa blue for positive and red for negative potential. The interface with M17 (depicted as gray cartoon) is bipolar, with red at the top and blue below. (B) The complex is rotated by 180  on the y-axis relative to panel A, with the surface of M17 colored according to electrostatics and fVa depicted as gray cartoon. A complementary bipolar surface is presented, with blue at the top and red at the bottom. Domains are labeled for clarity. Images were created using Pymol.

A stereo representation of the final coordinates and a sharpened map is depicted in Figure 5A, with statistics provided in supplemental Table 1. The interface between fVa and fXa is extensive, with a total buried surface area (BSA) of 4900 A2, involving 19 hydrogen bonds and 10 salt bridges (lists of all interactions are provided in supplemental Tables 3 and 4). The SP domain of fXa mediates the bulk of the interaction with fVa, contributing 66% of total BSA. Three regions of the SP domain are involved in the interface with fVa: the HBS comprising residues 59 to 126 and 230 to 244; the 130-helix comprising residues 129 to 134; and the 170-helix comprising residues 164 to 179. The light chain contributes the remaining 34% of the interaction interface, with most mediated by the EGF2 domain. The fVa interface is balanced between the A2 domain, A3 domain, and a2-loop, contributing 31%, 35%, and 34% to the BSA, respectively. The side chains of 12 of the M17 mutations are defined in the map. Of the 17 total mutations, 12 appear to improve the interaction with fVa, 2 have no apparent effect, 2 are outside the contact distance of 5 A, and 1 is likely to be worse than the WT residue (supplemental Table 5). The most important mutations for improving affinity for fVa appear to be S90R (Figure 5B), E129N (Figure 5C), and T132K (Figure 5D). Each of these increases the basic nature of the face of fXa that interacts with fVa. The interface is remarkably polar in nature (Figure 6), with the A2 domain, a2-loop, and top of the A3 domain forming a large, contiguous acidic surface that interacts with a highly basic surface of the SP and EGF2 domains. The 7 mutations in the EGF2 domain result in a net charge increase of +5 and the mutations in the SP domain increase the net charge by +2. This increase in positive electrostatic potential (supplemental Figure 4), rather than improvement of specific interactions, is likely the main reason for the increased affinity of M17 for fVa.
Discussion

It is well documented that fXa can interact with fVa in the absence of PL and that the resulting complex activates prothrombin faster than fXa on its own. It has also been demonstrated that at saturating concentrations, PL-free prothrombinase processes prothrombin down the meizothrombin pathway. Therefore, in theory, it should be possible to obtain particles of prothrombinase on a cryo-EM grid using WT proteins without the addition of PL, provided high concentrations are used to drive complex formation. A recent study reported on a cryo-EM structure of prothrombinase with prothrombin in the absence of PL; surprisingly, the grids were set up using extremely low protein concentrations. We repeated the reported grid conditions and obtained only empty grids, and we then increased the concentration 10-fold and observed a protein soup with no distinct particles. We also generated grids using WT fXa and fVa under the conditions used to obtain the map of M17-prothrombinase, but at a higher ratio of fXa to drive complex formation. However, processing these images did not result in any meaningful output, with particles appearing too small to represent the prothrombinase complex (supplemental Figure 5). We concluded that WT prothrombinase is not amenable to cryo-EM methodology in the absence of PL due to the low affinity of the fXa-fVa interaction. To improve affinity, we made 17 mutations to fXa, resulting in a dissociation constant for fVa of ~20nM. This effort was guided by a model of prothrombinase based on the orthologous snake venom complex, pseutarin C, and the sequence differences between human fXa and a high-affinity snake venom fXa ortholog, hopsarin D. Here, we further characterized the binding of M17 to fVa and found that the improvement over WT fXa is primarily due to an increased rate of association. We also demonstrated that prothrombin processing by M17-prothrombinase is independent of PL. This supports the conclusion that the main role of the PL surface in prothrombinase function is to increase the affinity of fXa for fVa. A structure of membrane-free M17-prothrombinase should therefore possess the features of WT prothrombinase required for prothrombin processing.

A possible concern is that the 17 mutations made to fXa might have altered its interface with fVa; however, the extent of the interface (4900 A2) renders this unlikely. In addition, the crystal structure of an orthologous prothrombinase with only ~60% sequence identity to human prothrombinase, pseutarin C, is essentially identical to the structure of M17 fXa with human fVa (root mean square deviation of 1.27 A, not including C-domains; supplemental Figure 6A). The fact that we designed M17 based on a model of human prothrombinase based on pseutarin C further supports the conservation of the general architecture. In addition, the AlphaFold-predicted structure of WT human prothrombinase is remarkably similar to the M17-prothrombinase structure reported here, with a root mean square deviation of 1.14 A (not including the C1, C2, Gla, or EGF1 domains; supplemental Figure 6B). Therefore, we acknowledge that the specifics of side-chain interactions will be different around the mutation sites; however, the interfacing regions and relative orientation of the 2 proteins are unlikely to be affected by the 17 mutations.

The M17-prothrombinase structure is also in good agreement with the bulk of the results from biochemical and mutagenesis studies. A PISA analysis of the interface provided a list of the residues that contribute most to the energy of binding (supplemental Table 6). The most important residues in the heavy chain of fVa are Y*665 and F668, both of which are in the a2-loop. The loss of sulfation has been shown to reduce peak thrombin generation by threefold due to a lowering of the affinity for fXa, supporting the importance of the interactions involving Y*665. The sequential truncation of the a2-loop from 709 to 699, 692, or 678 was found to have no impact on the cofactor activity of fVa; however, when the acidic region from 659 to 678 was removed, only 1% of clotting activity remained due to a 20-fold reduction in affinity for fXa. Similar results were found when the acidic region 659 to 663 was mutated to either Ala or Lys. In our structure, the N-terminal acidic region of the a2-loop interacts with the HBS of fXa. This is consistent with what we found for pseutarin C, the AlphaFold prediction, and a 1.2 A crystal structure of fXa with an a2-peptide, as well as with studies where the HBS mutations in fXa result in reduced affinity for fVa. These include R125, K236, and K240, all of which are observed to interact with the a2-loop in the M17-prothrombinase structure. Recently, an aptamer has been described that binds to fXa with high affinity and is able to reduce the fVa interaction to undetectable levels; the crystal structure of the fXa-aptamer complex later revealed exclusive interactions with the HBS in a manner that would only block the a2-loop interaction.

The most important residues in the SP domain of fXa were found to be R165 and M169 according to PISA, consistent with independent mutagenesis studies. These residues have been mistakenly considered part of the HBS of fXa, but belong to the spatially distinct 170-helix. In the structure, they interact exclusively with the A2 domain, including residues R510, A511, A512, D513, D577, and D578, all of which were found to be important interacting residues according to site-directed glycosylation and mutagenesis studies. The importance of the A2 domain is well-known because its removal by activated protein C (APC) inactivates prothrombinase. APC cleaves at Arg306 and Arg506, both of which are required for full inactivation. Arg306 is not at the interface with fXa and is available for cleavage when prothrombinase is assembled, but Arg506 is protected by fXa from APC cleavage. Although Arg506 is just outside the 5 A distance cutoff for the definition of an interacting residue, the loop it belongs to makes intimate contacts with M17 and is sterically protected from APC cleavage.

Comparison of M17-prothrombinase with prothrombinase from 7TPP. (A) A cartoon depiction of M17-prothrombinase (fVa in gray, the Gla and EGF1 domains of M17 [fXa] in light cyan, and the serine protease domain colored from blue to red from the N- to C-terminus). The a2-loop is colored magenta and labeled. (B) The same representation of the prothrombinase component of 7TPP is shown, with the translation and rotation of fXa indicated. The N-terminus of the serine protease domain of fXa is indicated. (C) A stereo view of the top of M17-prothrombinase (colored as above) with the a2-loop positioned as in 7TPP (residues 657-709) illustrates the overlap that renders the 2 structures incompatible. Images were created using Pymol.

In 2022, a cryo-EM structure of prothrombinase was published at a reported resolution of 4.1 A (protein data bank ID: 7TPP). Although 7TPP is grossly similar to the M17-prothrombinase structure reported here, it is different in important ways. When the fVa components are superimposed, the magnitude of the difference in the position of fXa becomes evident; the centroid of the heavy chain of the SP domain is shifted by 7.8 A and is rotated by ~10  (Figure 7A,B). This shift in the position of fXa coincides with a radically different placement of the a2-loop. A close-up of the top of the M17-prothrombinase complex with the a2-loop taken from 7TPP illustrates the incompatibility of its position in 7TPP with that of M17 in our structure (Figure 7C). The a2-loop position in our structure is supported by a higher-quality and -resolution cryo-EM map, the AlphaFold predictions, and a high-resolution crystal structure of an a2-peptide with fXa. We consider our structure of M17-prothrombinase to more accurately reflect the actual structure of human prothrombinase, particularly with respect to the positioning of the important a2-loop.

In conclusion, we developed a high affinity variant of fXa with 17 mutations that allowed the formation of a functional prothrombinase complex in the absence of PL membranes. The higher affinity was required to obtain particles of prothrombinase through cryo-EM. The 3.3-A map is of sufficient quality to observe important details of the interaction between fXa and fVa, including the critical interaction of the a2-loop with the HBS of fXa. This work contributes to our understanding of the cofactor function of fVa in hemostasis.

passages.text: Phylogenomic Analysis of Deep-Branching Telonemid
Abstract

The evolutionary history of eukaryotic supergroups has been investigated primarily by large-scale phylogenomics, but one major hindrance to continued progress is that some major eukaryotic groups have extremely sparse sampling. The phylum Telonemia is one such group. Environmental sampling shows two major subgroups of Telonemia, but there are only multigene phylogenomic data from three closely related species belonging to one of the subgroups, TEL1. Here, a single cell was isolated from the pelagic Pacific Ocean, which SSU phylogenetic analysis reveals to be a telonemid of the TEL2 subgroup and distantly related to telonemids with multigene sequence data. Through single-cell transcriptome sequencing and phylogenomic analysis, we investigate the impact of this new telonemid on the relation of Telonemia to the Stramenopila-Alveolata-Rhizaria supergroup (SAR) and other sparsely sampled or historically unstable supergroups, namely, Hemimastigophora, Provora, and Haptista. Our maximum-likelihood (ML) analysis supports Telonemia as sister to Hemimastigophora, together as sister to SAR, with Haptista and Provora forming a clade and sister to all three. However, our Bayesian analysis failed to converge on a topology. Throughout different Telonemia sampling, gene sampling, alignment trimming, and site removal schemes, the sisterhood of Telonemia and Hemimastigophora remained largely supported in ML trees, even when their sisterhood to SAR dissolved, as was the sisterhood of Haptista and Provora. Inclusion of our TEL2 telonemid largely did not influence these relationships. However, our results also highlight the unstable placements of aforementioned groups throughout variations of our data, of which subsets give results consistent with other previously published analyses of this scale.

A confident understanding of eukaryotic supergroup relationships is a prerequisite to study the deep evolutionary history of eukaryotes. A crucial shortcoming of multigene phylogenomic analyses of eukaryotic supergroups is the lack of taxon sampling in many major lineages. An example of this is the Telonemia phylum, of which only three closely related species have adequate sequence data for phylogenomic analysis. This study presents transcriptomic data from a fourth, early-diverging telonemid cell. We investigate the placement of Telonemia within eukaryotes, including the robustness of this placement throughout variations of data processing and subsampling. Our results support an alternative placement of Telonemia with group Hemimastigophora, together sister to SAR, conflicting with some previous studies.
Introduction

The phylum Telonemia is a historically poorly represented group of microbial eukaryotes. For nearly a century, only a single species was known: Telonema subtilis, with the second species, T. antarcticum, only described in 2005, and later renamed Lateronema antarcticum. Environmental SSU rDNA sequences have nevertheless revealed a cosmopolitan distribution for both marine and freshwater telonemids, and SSU phylogenies suggest ~20 subgroups falling into two major subdivisions: TEL1 including T. subtilis and TEL2 including L. antarcticum. Six additional species were recently described, all belonging to the TEL1 clade, so L. antarcticum remains the only described species in the TEL2 clade.

Multigene phylogenomic analyses are currently restricted to three telonemid species in the TEL1 clade: Telonema subtilis, Arpakorses versatilis, and Arpakorses idiomastiga. This is unfortunate because all data show telonemids to be only distantly related to other eukaryotes, and their specific relationships to other major eukaryotic groups remain contentious. Recent multigene phylogenies including TEL1 species suggest they are sister to the SAR supergroup (Stramenopila, Alveolata, and Rhizaria), leading to the proposal of a TSAR supergroup. However, other analyses place Telonemia as sister to Hemimastigophora or with Haptista (Haptophyta + Centroheliozoa), either of which together branch as sister to SAR. Hemimastigophora is a similarly poorly represented group, with sequence data from only two species available and multigene phylogenies placing them as sister to telonemids, but alternatively as sister to Cryptista, Archaeplastida, Haptista, and TSAR collectively or to Haptista and TSAR. Haptista has also been found to be related to TSAR or Cryptista and Archaeplastida. Another new group, the Provora, has also been found to be sister to Haptista and TSAR in a study that summed up this confusing situation by showing several conflicting topologies among Hemimastigophora, Haptista, Provora, Telonemia, and SAR among maximum-likelihood (ML) and Bayesian Inference (BI) trees.

Telonemids are one focal point of these debates, and the lack of data from diverse members of the group is a potential source of bias. Here, we reexamine the position of telonemids using the first available transcriptome from a representative of the TEL2 clade, derived from a single cell manually isolated from pelagic water from the Pacific Ocean. We show that TEL1 and TEL2 are monophyletic and together form a highly supported clade with Hemimastigophora, both branching sister to SAR. We also examine the impacts of gene sampling, trimming algorithms, Telonemia subsampling, and removal of fast-evolving sites.
Results and Discussion
Cell Telonemia sp. DSEL18 Is a Member of the TEL2 Clade

A single cell (DSEL18) with the overall appearance of a telonemid (Fig. S1) was isolated from water collected at 190 m depth in Monterey Bay and had its transcriptome sequenced. An SSU rRNA ML phylogeny including sequences from diverse Telonemia subgroups confirmed this cell to be a telonemid (Fig. S2). DSEL18 fell in the 2j subgroup of TEL2 (65% bootstrap support (BS)), making it the only taxon in TEL2 with transcriptome data and distinct from the only species in TEL2 that has been described, L. antarcticum, a member of subgroup 2k (Fig. S2).
Phylogenomic Placement of TEL2 Telonemids

For phylogenomic analyses, we first selected 109 eukaryotes and 233 proteins (see Materials and Methods), of which 78/233 (33%) were present in Telonemia sp. DSEL18, resulting in the final concatenated alignment with 13,687 out of 57,444 sites (24%) present in this taxon when alignments are trimmed with Block Mapping and Gathering with Entropy (BMGE), which removes high-entropy sites (Fig. 1), or 15,196 of 73,229 sites (21%) present when trimmed with trimAl, which removes sites by gap thresholds (Fig. S3). The overall topology of ML trees based on this data is largely congruent with many previously published phylogenomic studies, with a few notable exceptions. One exception is the clade composed of apusomonad Thecamonas trahens and CruMs member Mantamonas plastica. In previous analyses, Apusomonadida are within the supergroup Obazoa, and CruMs are monophyletic and sister to both Obazoa and Amoebozoa. A note on this inconsistency is included in the Supplementary material. Another exception is that Provora is a sister to Haptista, which is inconsistent with previous analyses where Provora branched with Hemimastigophora in many analyses, although not in all.

Maximum-likelihood tree inferred from 233 BMGE-trimmed proteins and 109 taxa under the LG + C60 + F + R + PMSF model of evolution, with LG + C20 + F + R used as the guide tree. Node values show nonparametric bootstrap support out of 200 (top) and ultrafast bootstrap support out of 1,000 (bottom). Circles represent ultrafast bootstrap support of >=98% and nonparametric bootstrap support of >=90%. Scale bar represents estimated amino acid substitutions per site. Branches labeled with 2x have been scaled to half their original length. Bar graph on the left shows the percent of genes and individual sites of each taxon.

The monophyly of telonemids was completely supported in our phylogenomic analysis (Fig. 1, Fig. S3), and this group branched with Hemimastigophora with high support (95% BS, 96% UFB). This clade was in turn sister to SAR with stronger support (98% BS, 97% UFB, collectively referred to as HT + SAR), similar to a topology reported previously based on analyses including three TEL1 telonemids.
Testing the Placement of Telonemids

Given the various positions found for telonemids in different published analyses, we re-examined the results by removing Telonemia sp. DSEL18, retaining only the telonemid with the highest coverage (96% site coverage), and removing all telonemids. In parallel, we also compared the effect of trimming alignments with BMGE or trimAl and of different site coverage thresholds for protein selection. ML analyses of most of these variants recovered H + T with high support, and inclusion of Telonemia sp. DSEL18 largely did not influence the placement of telonemids in our dataset (Fig. 2a). When H + T was favored, it was most often sister to SAR. Haptista was also most often supported as the sister to Provora. Notably, the choice of trimming method produced dramatic differences in placements of Hemimastigophora, Provora, and Haptophyta only when sparser genes were included:TrimAl-trimmed 262 gene datasets were the only ones to recover TSAR, Haptista + TSAR, and place Hemimastigophora sister to Provora (Fig. 2a, Figs. S4 to S7, Table S3).

a) Impact of protein sampling, Telonemia sampling, and trimming algorithm on placements of various groups. Bars indicate summarized ultrafast bootstrap support (out of 1,000) of relevant nodes from ML trees inferred by LG + C60 + F + R + PMSF models, with LG + C20 + F + R used for the guide tree. Maximum missing positions refers to the threshold used for protein selection. Asterisks note that an additional four proteins were added past this threshold, with <=50% missing positions in at least three out of four telonemids. Numbers above the graphs indicate the number of alignment sites. Tel, Telonemia; Hemi, Hemimastigophora; Hapt, Haptista; Prov, Provora; Crypt, Cryptista; Vir, Viridiplantae; Gla, Glaucophyta; Rho, Rhodophyta; Disc, Discoba; Ob, Obazoa; Mal, Malawimonada. When no telonemids are included, "Hemi + Tel" refers solely to Hemimastigophora. b) Stepwise removal of fast- and heterotachously evolving sites from an original alignment of 233 BMGE-trimmed proteins with 55,744 sites. Each step represents the removal of the top 3,000 sites. All trees were inferred under LG + C60 + F + R + PMSF models with 1,000 ultrafast bootstraps, with LG + C20 + F + R used for the guide tree.

Comparing these results to previous analyses that include at least Telonemia and Hemimastigophora, we see a wide range of outcomes, with overlapping results in subsets of our variants and published analyses. For example, Haptista + TSAR and Hemimastigophora + Provora were both recovered in our largest datasets (>88,000 sites) and in. Similarly, found Hemimastigophora sister to Haptista + TSAR or Hemimastigophora + Diaphoretickes depending on the data used, which both also appeared in our variant data sets. The results of match ours most consistently, as the HT + SAR relationship is recovered in most of our comparisons. Interestingly, despite this consistency, our dataset and that of contain less overlap (166 genes, 156 in telonemids) than those of and Tikhonenkov et al. (202 and 257 overlapped genes, 186 and 238 in telonemids, respectively) (Table S3). On the other hand, the results of, whose dataset is a subset of, are most dissimilar, potentially due to their inclusion of the newly sequenced Meteora sporadica, which they placed sister to Hemimastigophora, and their lack of multiple Provora. In their study, Telonemia and Hemimastigophora placements differ between trees with different taxa, but in no case support TSAR or Hemimastigophora + Telonemia, nor was Haptista placed with provorid Ancoracysta.

We also examined UF bootstrap support over the stepwise removal of fast-evolving and heterotachously evolving (evolving under different rates across lineages) sites from our original 233-gene, BMGE-trimmed ML matrix (Fig. 2b). In both analyses, the H + T relationship was more robust to site removal than that of HT + SAR. In fast-site removal, TSAR becomes strongly supported after H + T falls in support at ~30% site removal, whereas in heterotachous-site removal, TSAR is at no point highly supported. In heterotachous-site removal, the larger grouping of Haptista + Provora with HT + SAR loses support very quickly, after which Haptista and Provora are strongly supported as placed in a clade with Archaeplastida + Cryptista (Fig. 2b).
Bayesian Inference

Using the 233-gene alignment subsampled to 81 taxa, Bayesian inference (BI) was conducted under the model CAT-GTR+Gamma4. We ran four independent Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains, and consensus trees were summarized from >15,000 trees (10% burn-in) (Fig. S8). However, no two chains converged, and placements of Telonemia, Hemimastigophora, Haptista, and Provora were all inconsistent. We then employed the more computationally efficient CAT-poisson+Gamma4 model, summarizing from >10,000 trees (10% burn-in) (Fig. S2). Under this model, only chains 1 and 4 achieved a maximum difference less than 1 (maxdiff 0.39, meandiff 0.007). TSAR was supported in all chains (PP 1), and Haptista + TSAR converged in three out of four chains. Hemimastigophora + Diaphoretickes also converged in three out of four chains (posterior probability of 1).
Conclusion

Overall, our results question the validity of the TSAR supergroup to the exclusion of Hemimastigophora, and more broadly demonstrate the instability of Telonemia, Hemimastigophora, Provora, and Haptista based on current datasets. These groups often branch near each other on the tree of eukaryotes, usually with high support, but topologies remain conflicting between different analyses.

One factor that emerges from these analyses is the length of the concatenations. and both include >90,000 sites and recover TSAR in both ML and BI analyses, while and, each with 70 to 73,000 sites, do not. Our ML analyses only recover TSAR in our longest concatenations, >88,000 sites. Choice of trimming can also influence results, and in our dataset is most influential when all genes are included:however, Lax et al. and Tikhonenkov et al. both use BMGE, while we recover TSAR in trimAl-trimmed matrices only. Additionally, our gene dataset, even when sampled to fewer genes, contains more overlap with these datasets than that of, ruling this out as a source of bias toward the HT + SAR topology in shorter alignments.

An investigation by into the monophyly of Archaeplastida across datasets found that longer datasets resulted in more topological consistency than various subsets of genes and taxa. This trend may extend to inconsistencies found here. For instance, it is possible that longer datasets discussed here contain more phylogenetically informative sites that better counteract fast-site noise affecting TSAR support in shorter datasets, as in our 233-gene ML tree (Fig. 2b), TSAR is favoured over HT + SAR after removal of ~35% of the fastest-evolving sites, and HT + SAR also falls in support in after removal of the ~25% fastest-evolving sites. However, as nodes with sparse taxon sampling are particularly susceptible to nonphylogenetic signal, to which longer datasets are not impervious, it is likely that trends will not become clear until denser taxon sampling is feasible in phyla that currently have few representatives, in combination with careful construction of ultra-long phylogenomic datasets.
Materials and Methods
Single-Cell Isolation, Sequencing, and Transcriptome Assembly

Telonemia sp. DSEL18 was isolated during a research cruise by the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute. Water was sampled at 34.286N, -127.355W on 2018 January 30 at a depth of 190 m using an SBE 9plus conductivity-temperature-depth rosette sampler (Sea-Bird Electronics). A single cell of Telonemia was identified by microscopy and placed in 2 microL of Smart-Seq2 lysis buffer at -80  C. cDNA was generated with the Smart-Seq2 protocol, from which libraries were prepared with Illumina Nextera XT and sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 550 platform. Reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic v0.39 (ILLUMINACLIP:TruSeq3-PE-2.fa:2:30:10:2:True LEADING:3 TRAILING:3 SLIDINGWINDOW:4:30 MINLEN:36) and assembled with rnaSPAdes v3.15.1. Transcript-coding regions were predicted using TransDecoder v5.5.0 (https://www.github.com/TransDecoder/), incorporating search results to UniProt Swiss-Prot and Pfam databases for coding region selection.
Phylogenetic Analyses

To obtain ribosomal SSU rDNA sequences, Telonemia SSU sequences were collected from NCBI Genbank and used as blastn queries to search against our transcriptome. For phylogenetic analysis, additional Telonemia SSU sequences were collected from SILVA. Sequences were clustered at 99% identity using CD-HIT, aligned with MAFFT-LINS-I v7, and trimmed with trimAl v1.2 (-gt 0.5). ModelFinder was run using IQ-TREE v2.1.0, which selected the TN + F + R3 model of evolution, which was run with 1,000 nonparametric bootstraps.

For multigene analysis, we built upon a preexisting dataset of 263 proteins with representatives across eukaryote diversity, to which new taxa (see Table S1) were added to this dataset by blastp search of proteomes. Hits with an e-value of <10-20 and 50% coverage were retained and searched with blastp to the UniProt Swiss-Prot database. Regions that did not align to Swiss-Prot curated proteins were trimmed using a custom script. Single-gene alignments of the 263 proteins and candidate additions from new taxa were made with MAFFT-LINS-I v7 and trimmed with trimAl (-gappyout). Single-gene trees were constructed in IQ-TREE v2.1.0 using the LG + G model with 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates, and each tree was visually inspected to remove contaminant, nonhomologous, and paralogous sequences from added taxa with FigTree (http://tree.bio.ed.ac.uk/software/figtree/). Clean sequences were aligned and trimmed as above, prior to calculation of taxon and protein alignment coverage using SCaFoS v1.2.5. A set of 109 taxa was selected to accommodate phylogenetic breadth across eukaryotes and higher site coverage per taxon in alignments, after which sequences were again realigned.

In total, 24 final matrices were subjected to ML analyses. Four different taxa sets were used by including either all telonemids, excluding the lowest-coverage telonemid, including only the single highest-coverage telonemid, or excluding all telonemids. For each, single-protein alignments were trimmed with BMGE (-BLOSUM30) or trimAl (-gappyout). From each trimming method, three sets of proteins were chosen. A supermatrix of all proteins and all species was made with SCaFoS for both trimming methods, and thresholds were chosen according to these output statistic ("out.stat") files. A "good" set contained proteins that had <=40% missing positions across all taxa in one of the trimming methods, with an additional four with <=50% missing positions in at least three out of four telonemids (233 proteins). A smaller set included only proteins with <= 30% missing positions (192 proteins). A larger set included all proteins in our dataset, excluding one very low-coverage protein (262 proteins). Selected proteins were then realigned and retrimmed with only selected taxa.

All ML analyses were done in IQ-TREE v2.1.0 under the evolutionary model LG + C60 + F + R + PMSF (Posterior Mean Site Frequencies) (-m LG + C60 + F + R -ft ), using guide trees generated by command -m LG + C20 + F + R -bb 1000, done separately for each tree inferred. Nonparametric bootstrap support was found for both BMGE- and TrimAl-trimmed 233-gene matrices. The BMGE 233-gene matrix was the starting matrix for removal of fast-evolving and heterotachously evolving sites, which were removed using PhyloFisher tools fast_site_remover.py and heterotachy.py with default settings. Ultrafast bootstrap support for nodes of interest was found using the CONSENSE program from PHYLIP v3.697 on IQ-TREE.UFBoot output files, generated by option --boot-trees. The BMGE 233-gene matrix was also used for BI analysis. For computational feasibility, a smaller subset of 81 species was used by selecting the best-represented taxa from each phylum. BI was conducted using PhyloBayes-MPI under CAT-GTR+Gamma4 (mpirun -np 32 pb_mpi -d -cat -gtr -S -dgam 4 ) and CAT-Poisson+Gamma4 models (mpirun -np 32 pb_mpi -d -cat -poisson -S -dgam 4 ). Four MCMC chains were run simultaneously until each generated 15,000 or 10,000 trees, respectively, taking 2 to 3 months. Consensus trees were found by bpcomp, applying a 10% burn-in and subsampling every 10 trees. Larger burn-ins of up to ~50% were attempted but did not affect the convergence of chains.
